opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the more interesting failure modes we see, and it comes down to what a latent action actually is in a model like Genie. We never give the model ground-truth action labels. It learns a small discrete vocabulary of actions purely from watching video, by figuring out which compact code best explains the change between one frame and the next. So the meaning of an action isn't fixed the way "press left" is fixed in a real game. It's whatever was most predictive of frame-to-frame change in the training data.

That has a couple of consequences once you roll the model out for a long time. First, the latent actions are learned in context. The model is always interpreting an action relative to the recent history it's conditioned on. Early in a rollout, that history looks a lot like the training distribution, so a given code reliably maps to something like "move right." But as you keep generating, you're feeding the model its own outputs, and small errors pile up. The scene drifts, the character might blur or shift slightly, the background changes in ways that weren't quite consistent. Eventually the context no longer looks like the situations where that action code was learned, so the mapping from code to effect gets weaker or ambiguous.

Second, there's a data issue. In the videos we train on, people don't usually hold one direction forever. Movement tends to come in fairly short bursts, with stops, jumps, and changes of direction. So the model has seen relatively few examples of the same action sustained over a long horizon. When you keep pressing the same latent action, you're asking for something that's underrepresented, and the model starts falling back on what it thinks is likely to happen next, like slowing down, stopping, or doing something else plausible, rather than continuing to follow the action.

And there's a limited memory window. The model only attends over a certain number of past frames, so over a long rollout it loses track of things like momentum or the larger layout of the level. All of that together means the action signal gets outweighed by the model's prior about what usually happens in a video.

So we don't really think of it as the action breaking. It's more that the model's world-modeling prior gradually overwhelms the controllability signal as you move away from the training distribution. Fixing that is a big part of the work: longer context, more diverse and longer-horizon data, and training objectives that more explicitly reward consistent, controllable responses to actions, not just realistic-looking frames.

r001.rationale: The response says the model prior can outweigh controllability and mentions losing track of momentum, but it does not say learned physical momentum overrides a latent action requesting a sudden reversal.

r002.rationale: The response says long stretches of one action are underrepresented in training. It does not attribute ignored direction changes to such changes being uncommon in the training behavior policies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite things to talk about, because it gets at what the latent actions actually are. The way we train Genie, the action space is completely unsupervised. We never tell the model "action three means move right." We just have this latent action model that looks at a frame and the next frame and has to compress whatever changed into one of a small number of discrete codes, like eight of them. The dynamics model then has to predict the next frame given the current frame and that code. So the only pressure on the latent action is to be the most useful piece of information for explaining what's about to happen.

What falls out of that is that the latents tend to be consistent across a lot of settings, which honestly surprised us. You can take action three in one game and it moves the character right, and you do it in a totally different environment that the model has never seen, and it moves the character right there too. But "consistent" and "a hard-coded controller" are not the same thing. The latent is really capturing something like "the kind of change that usually happens next in this context," and the context can shift under you as you keep going.

So when you hold an action for a long time and it stops doing what you expect, there are usually a few things going on. One is just data distribution. In the videos we train on, when a character moves in one direction for a while, they typically hit something. They run into a wall, they reach the edge of the level, the camera stops scrolling, they jump. Prolonged uninterrupted movement in a single direction is actually kind of rare in the data, so once you've been going right for twenty or thirty frames you've drifted into a region where the model's priors about what happens next are different, and the latent that meant "right" in the common case can get reinterpreted as, I don't know, "stop" or "turn around," because that's what tends to happen there.

The second thing is that the model is autoregressive and it's imagining the world, not simulating it. Every frame is conditioned on its own previous outputs, so small errors compound. The character might get slightly blurry, the background might start to repeat in a way that doesn't quite make physical sense, and at some point the model loses track of what's foreground and what's background. If it loses the character, then the latent action has nothing clean to act on. It's still trying to apply some change, but the thing it's changing isn't what you think it is anymore.

And the third piece is that the codebook is small and the actions are somewhat entangled. A single latent might be encoding movement plus some camera behavior plus some animation state. Early on those are all aligned and it looks like a clean "move right." Over a long rollout the different components can come apart, so you'd see the camera keep going but the character stall, or vice versa.

I think the honest framing is that Genie learned controllability as an emergent property of video prediction, and the failure modes are the places where the video prediction prior and the control intention disagree. For us that was actually a really useful signal. It tells you where the world model's understanding of persistence and object permanence is weak, and those are exactly the things we've been trying to push on with longer context and more consistent memory in the follow-up work.

r001.rationale: The response attributes reversals or stops to shifted training priors, autoregressive errors, and entangled codes; it does not say learned physical momentum overrides a latent requesting a sudden reversal.

r002.rationale: It says prolonged uninterrupted movement in one direction is rare in training videos, but does not say direction changes were uncommon in the behavior policies or that this explains ignoring a latent requesting a direction change.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about that as a limitation of how the latent actions are learned. They’re inferred from changes between video frames, rather than grounded in an explicit command like “move left.” So an action can appear to correspond to a particular direction without having that meaning consistently across every state.

As you roll the model forward, small prediction errors can accumulate, or you can reach states that are less well represented in the training data. The same latent action might then stop producing the change you expect. From that behavior alone, though, we can’t tell whether the action’s interpretation has become inconsistent or whether the dynamics model is failing to predict its effect.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the effect to latent actions lacking consistent meaning across states and to accumulated prediction errors or unfamiliar states; it does not propose learned physical momentum overriding a sudden reversal request.

r002.rationale: It mentions underrepresented training states, but does not say direction changes were uncommon in the training behavior policies or that this caused Genie to ignore the latent action.

sol-6.1.text: I’d think of that as a limitation of how Genie learns its actions. It learns latent actions from video rather than from explicit labels like “move left” or “move right,” so their meaning depends on the visual context. After a long sequence of movement, the model can drift into a state where the same latent action no longer produces the change you expect. Small prediction errors can accumulate, too. So an action that initially looks like a reliable direction control isn’t necessarily a consistent control across every state or over a long rollout.

r001.rationale: The response mentions accumulated prediction errors and state-dependent drift, but does not say that learned physical momentum overrides a latent action requesting a sudden reversal.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute missed direction changes to such changes being uncommon in the training behavior policies.
